title: GPX Elevation Gain Calculator: Total Climb
description: Sum the positive elevation changes in a GPX track with the GPX Elevation Gain Calculator — total ascent from the recording itself. Free, local.
summary_sentence: For example, a climb profile stepping 100 → 112 → 108 → 125 → 121 → 140 metres gains 48 metres: the three rises (12 + 17 + 19) counted, the two dips ignored.
quick_answer: The GPX Elevation Gain Calculator adds up every positive elevation change between consecutive points in a GPX file to give the total ascent. Load the file and read the climb — what 'how much up was there?' actually means, computed from your recording itself.

body.t: The guidebook says 800 m of climbing; your recording's gain says what the day actually held. Its mirror is the
Barometric watches, GPS-altitude phones and map-corrected platforms produce three different gains from one walk. The raw-file sum is the baseline the arguments start from.
Weekly climbing totals drive hill training. A consistent from-the-file method beats whichever app you happened to sync with.
Gain per distance is a difficulty language: 48 m over 2 km is a stroll; 1,000 m over 10 km is a serious day. The ratio starts here.

examples.label: Example · The sum, step by step

body.t: Elevations 100, 112, 108, 125, 121, 140: rises are +12, +17, +19 = 48 m of gain; the falls (−4, −4) belong to the loss calculator. Net change is only +40 m — which is why 'net' is the wrong number for effort.

GPS altitude jitter of ±3 m between points manufactures phantom climbs on flat ground — hundreds of false metres over a long track. Platforms smooth or threshold this away, which is why their gains differ from a raw sum like this one.

popular_table.note: For any profile: gain − loss = net change, always. If a platform's numbers break that identity, it filtered something — usually small wiggles, by a threshold it should disclose.

faq: Does it smooth the elevation first?

This calculator sums the recorded steps as they stand, so you see the file's own arithmetic. Smoothing and thresholding are platform choices that lower gain — knowing the raw sum tells you how much they removed.
They contribute no step. A file with sparse elevation (only some points stamped) understates gain — the count of elevation-bearing points is part of an honest reading.
Barometric series are smoother (weather drift aside); GPS altitude is noisier, inflating raw gain more. The calculator sums whichever the file carries — the source is the story.
Both units are reported, per this site's US/Europe convention — climbs are quoted in feet by American hikers and metres by European ones.
Route elevations often come from a map model when the route was planned — gain over a planned route is the model's promise; over a recorded track, the day's evidence.
Many platforms ignore rises below a few metres to defeat noise. Their gain will read lower than this raw sum, by design — neither is wrong, they are different definitions.
